title: Clear what people are waiting on before your own list
detail: David addressed Peyton's ECA comments on 10/20 at 3:07 pm; you replied "will get back to you tomorrow", promised it again at standup 10/21 and 10/22, and the V2 feedback landed 10/22 at 6:44 pm. That's two and a half days of David's design-to-dev runway, and the Design Review is now due Monday. Your own work moves fast (Olson was off Webflow a day early); the bottleneck is the reviews only you can give.
try: Starting Monday, open your standup turn with "Who's waiting on me?" and give each a time today. Anything a teammate hands you for review gets an answer within one working day, even if the answer is "Wednesday, here's why."
source: Simon Sinek, Leaders Eat Last: a leader's job is to take care of the people doing the work, so they can focus on it.

title: Renegotiate due dates instead of rolling them
detail: At midnight on 10/23, 13 of your Asana tasks moved to "Today" within one minute, leaving 17 open tasks all due today. madak.com WORK has moved four times since 10/19 and madak.com Pricing three times. When every date rolls, nobody (including you) can see which ones are real, and your 10/21 commitment to "3 or 4 small Madak tasks" quietly missed.
try: This afternoon, pick the five tasks that truly matter next week and give the rest an honest date or move them to a Someday section. If a task rolls twice, cut its scope or hand it off rather than moving it a third time.
source: Basecamp, Shape Up (Ryan Singer): fix the time you're willing to spend (the appetite) and cut scope to fit, rather than letting work run on.

title: Make every handoff carry its own context
detail: Four handoffs this week arrived missing something: the NCCET Hour Tracker went to Elli with no note (10/20), Elli forgot the SafeTraces attachments (10/21), Josh sent David the Luis De Souza Pinto page with no explanation (10/22), and Sponsor Cards bounced David to Kolya to Adam and back in seven minutes over two unnamed logos (10/22). Each one cost a round-trip and someone's focus.
try: At Monday's full-team meeting, propose a three-line handoff note for any task passed to the build team: what's done, what's needed, where the files are. Save it as an Asana task template so strategists can start from it.

title: Answer the AI worry directly
detail: When you showed Claude Design on 10/20, Jamie said "there goes my job" and David said he didn't know how to feel about it. You answered with your own excitement, which is real, but not their worry. Meanwhile your plans give each of them a bigger role: Jamie as brand reviewer on every Webflow migration over the next six months, David moving into the Astro builds.
try: In next week's 1:1s, tell each of them plainly how their role grows (Jamie: brand owner on every refresh, starting with Olson; David: Astro builds and the visual editor research), then ask which skill they want to get better at this quarter.
source: Brené Brown, Dare to Lead: clear is kind, and leaving people to fill in the blanks about their future is unkind.

title: Check Jamie's load before Wednesday
detail: Jamie is out 10/29 and 10/30, and the following are all aimed at Wednesday 10/28: the Olson brand presentation for the 12/2 board, the JMU graphic that Adam turned into a full brand presentation on 10/21, about nine SafeTraces web app screens, two USA Youth one-pagers and your Olson site review. Requests come from Adam, Elli, Josh and you, and SafeTraces already slipped once for Josh's last-minute GMU deck on 10/21.
try: On Monday, list Jamie's week with her, rank it together, and agree with Adam which item moves past 10/28. Take your Olson site review off her critical path by pushing it to the week of 11/2.

title: Point David at Sanity's Presentation tool first
detail: On 10/22 you asked David to find a Webflow-style click-to-edit layer for the Astro sites by 10/30. Sanity already does this: its Presentation tool and Visual Editing add click-to-edit overlays on a live preview, and the @sanity/astro integration supports it. madak.com already runs on Astro and Sanity, so it's a ready test bed.
try: Give David a narrower brief: set up Presentation on one madak.com page in the Studio, have a strategist change a headline and an image, and report back by 10/30 on whether it's simple enough for clients.

title: Close the week with what shipped
detail: A lot shipped this week and most of it passed quietly: Olson off Webflow ahead of plan (10/20), the JMU update page live the same evening (10/21), Stanwood Camano fully closed out (10/21), Madison Design Build site health from 82 to 90, the Western season program to print and the pre-order banner live in 38 minutes (10/22). Standups only look ahead to the next commitment, so nobody sees the whole week at once.
try: At today's full-team meeting (and every Friday after), take five minutes: each build person names one thing they shipped this week and one person who helped them do it.
source: Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer, The Progress Principle: making progress on meaningful work is the strongest everyday boost to motivation, and it works best when people can see it.

title: Finish one of your builds before starting the next
detail: Between 10/27 and 10/29 you pitched or started the Agency OS, an Asana maintenance bot, a thin-task context bot, Ship Studio and Stacky evaluations, and built the Scribblio clone on the night of 10/28. Over the same nights, /strategic-roadmap & /proposal, Email Command Center and Claude Bootcamp were each re-dated four times (10/27 through 10/30), the growth strategy reached David a day late (10/29 a.m., so the 10/28 meeting moved to 11/2), and the Agency OS setup you named on 10/28 didn't happen. The energy is great for the team; the cost is that your own commitments are the ones that slip.
try: On Monday, name at standup the one personal build you'll finish this week, and don't start another until it ships or you've cut it. Put the three tasks that rolled all week on a real date or give them back to Adam.
source: Greg McKeown, Essentialism: doing fewer things, chosen deliberately, gets more of what matters done than spreading effort across everything.

title: Set a Monday triage for weekend requests
detail: David started the week with about 15 tasks Adam sent over the weekend (10/26), and by 10/29 he said the load was "definitely feeling like a lot." The SEO/AEO SOP has been open since 7/30 and re-dated on 10/1, 10/2, 10/9 and 10/27, and Adam's 10/13 ask to turn the Part Works audit into a task template has rolled about a dozen times. On 10/29 David agreed to a recurring 2-hour SEO/AEO block; nothing was on record by that evening.
try: Agree with Adam on Monday that build requests sent after Friday get their due dates set at Monday standup, not by the sender. In the same standup, have David put the weekly SEO/AEO block on his calendar while you're all on the call.
source: Cal Newport, Deep Work: protect focused time on the calendar in advance, or shallow, urgent work will fill every hour.

title: Check every figure before a data page goes to review
detail: The Gators /invest page changed hands about nine times between 10/27 and 10/30. On 10/28 at 6:37 pm Josh caught four errors at once: the ten-year endowment still showed $500,000, the women's gap bar used the men's numbers, every year label read May 2026, and the endowment button pointed to the wrong link. Adam was still sending final tweaks this morning. Donor pages carry real money and a client's credibility, so careless numbers cost more than a round-trip.
try: Add a figures check to the build team's definition of done for any page with numbers: paste the source (Adam's comment or the deck) and the staging link into Claude, ask it to list every figure that doesn't match, and write "figures checked" in the handoff comment. Start with the new Alumni Memories page.

title: Hand David the visual editor decision
detail: You asked David on 10/26 to evaluate Sanity, then reviewed Sanity Presentation yourself that day, demoed it on 10/27, and went on to Ship Studio and Stacky on 10/28. David's evaluation is still due today with no activity, and it's now mostly a second opinion on work you already did. Your open reminders say to bring David into the Astro builds and the editor; owning a decision does that better than another research task.
try: On Monday, give David the call: the criteria (strategists and clients can edit copy and CMS without help), the three candidates, and a date to recommend one at standup. Tell him you'll advise, not decide.
source: Daniel Pink, Drive: autonomy over the task, along with mastery and purpose, is what sustains motivation in creative work.

title: Have the builder show the launch
detail: You showed something at every standup this week: the client dashboard (10/26), Sanity Presentation and the AI-first plan (10/27, which ran over), the Agency OS plan (10/28) and the Scribblio clone (10/29). Meanwhile David's /invest page went live on gatorsrugby.com (10/29), he put Meyer's /give page live and the new hero on seven pages (10/28), and Jamie sent both Crusaders decks a day early (10/27). None of these were shown to the team. This builds on last week's Friday wins: seeing the live page lands harder than hearing its name.
try: Starting next Friday, give the team meeting a five-minute "show it live" slot: whoever shipped shares their screen and walks through it. Move your own demos into the same slot so standups stay on commitments.
source: Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer, The Progress Principle: visible progress on meaningful work is the strongest everyday driver of motivation.

title: Build Jamie a brand-locked deck skill
detail: On 10/28 Jamie named Google Slides as the part of her job she'd most like to lose, and you said it needs to be a bigger priority for you. On 10/27 she said Claude's PowerPoint exports come back with odd layouts, and she's been checking every page because fonts and colors change. Claude Skills can package a client's fonts, colors, logo rules and a master .pptx template, so Claude builds from the template instead of guessing.
try: Next week, spend 45 minutes with Jamie building a Skill for one client (Crusaders, since both decks are fresh). Then have her regenerate one slide from each deck and compare it with what she sent Adam.

title: Ask David which growth goal he'd bet against
detail: You sent David the growth strategy on 10/29 and asked whether the campaign goals are realistic or could be more aggressive; his answer was "All right." He's reviewing his own manager's plan, presented as nearly final, which makes candid pushback hard. Monday's 11/2 meeting is the moment that decides whether he treats this as his plan or yours.
try: Open Monday's meeting with one specific question: "Which goal would you bet against, and why?" Wait through the silence, then change at least one thing in the plan based on his answer and tell him you did.
source: Kim Scott, Radical Candor: ask for criticism with a specific question, stay quiet long enough for a real answer, and reward the candor so it keeps coming.

title: Send the task before standup ends
detail: The SEO/AEO report and dashboard layout task for David was yours to send on 11/2 ("sometime today"), again on 11/3 ("I'll do that after this meeting"), and Asana shows only two tasks created by you all week, neither of them his. The two-week AI task you promised David on 11/2 hasn't gone out either, while Jamie got hers on 11/3. On the same 11/3 call you told David that a week without answering Peyton isn't great; he has now waited a week on you.
try: Next week, when you say "I'll send you a task" at standup, make it before the call ends: dictate it to Claude or Asana while everyone is still on and confirm the person can see it. Start Monday with David's SEO/AEO report task and his AI task.
source: Simon Sinek, Leaders Eat Last: trust comes from leaders holding themselves to the standard they set, before asking it of others.

title: Close the loop on David's Peyton fix
detail: On 11/3 you told David in front of Jamie that Peyton's CAC comment had gone seven days without a reply. He took it straight on: he sent Peyton the hub and state template by 1:04 pm, answered each of her comments within about 35 minutes, and had CAC live on 11/3, two days before the Thursday launch. Nobody has told him the correction worked, and the last thing he heard on the topic was the criticism.
try: On Monday, tell David one-on-one that the CAC turnaround is exactly what you meant, naming the 35-minute replies. Next time a correction is needed, give it to him privately right after standup, not during it.
source: Kim Scott, Radical Candor: praise in public, criticize in private, and keep the feedback specific so people know what to repeat.

title: Keep standup running when you're out
detail: Only two standups were recorded this week (11/2 and 11/3). On 11/4 you had focus time and on 11/5 you were out from 11 to 1, so there's no record of what David and Jamie committed to. This morning you declined today's build team meeting and the team huddle too. The commitment loop holds the team together, and right now it only runs when you're on the call.
try: Make Wispr Flow record standup whoever opens it, and name a stand-in for next week (David Mon–Wed, Jamie Thu–Fri). The stand-in runs the same three questions: what landed, what's next, what's blocked. Tell them at Monday's standup.
source: Patrick Lencioni, Death by Meeting: a short daily check-in keeps a team aligned only if it happens every day, without fail.

title: Give the SEO/AEO SOP a fixed two hours
detail: David's SEO/AEO SOP task has been open since 7/30. Asana shows it untouched and overdue since 11/3, after he said on 11/2 and 11/3 that it was planned and he was "just really trying to tweak it." His content and AEO feedback on the growth plan was also due today. He's been shipping client work fast all week, so the trouble isn't effort: an internal doc with no end point keeps losing to client work and to polishing.
try: On Monday, agree with David on a two-hour appetite for v1: whatever exists at the end goes into Asana as-is (brain-dumped into Claude, as you suggested on 11/3) and he walks you through it at Tuesday's standup. Improvements go on a v2 list.
source: Ryan Singer, Shape Up (Basecamp): set an appetite, fix the time and let the scope flex, so the work ships instead of being polished indefinitely.

title: Give Jamie's brand weeks protected hours
detail: On 11/2 Jamie told you Wednesdays are when Adam "dumps everything" on her, and you moved the brand audit to 11/13 for that reason. The week went that way anyway: an annual report, Phinney Ridge's booklet, a same-day CAA print ad from Adam on 11/3, and WWU logos for Josh; she turned the ad and logos around in under an hour each. The audit has no Asana activity yet. And the "Designer of the Future" task you described as two weeks of thinking is due today, 11/6.
try: On Monday, put two 2-hour "Madak brand" holds on Jamie's calendar for Tuesday and Thursday, tell Adam at the team meeting that brand work is happening then, and move Designer of the Future to 11/16 so it matches the two weeks you promised.
source: Cal Newport, Deep Work: creative work needs blocks set aside in advance, or reactive requests will fill the week.

title: Celebrate the handoff, not just the builder
detail: The best moment of the week was a chain: on 11/4 Jamie fixed the Ride the Tide homepage image and caught a warped smile no one had asked about, Elli passed it along at 6:11 pm, and David had it live with a link back to her at 6:22 pm. CAC went live two days early because David cleared Peyton's sweep within a day of getting it. Recognition usually goes to whoever pushed publish, but these launches happened because each handoff was clean.
try: In next Friday's show-it-live slot, have Jamie and David walk the Ride the Tide fix together, from her file to his publish, and name each person in the chain. Ask the team which handoff they want to be that fast next.
source: Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer, The Progress Principle: people are most motivated by visible progress on meaningful work, and by others' help getting there.

title: Pilot Vercel comments on ECA before cutting Figma seats
detail: On 11/3 you laid out the plan: only the three of you keep Figma and Paper seats, and strategists and clients review working prototypes through Claude artifact links and Vercel's comment toolbar. ECA is the first build heading that way, to Vince this week. Vercel Comments on preview deployments are generally available, and you can invite people outside the team to view and comment. Running it once, on a real project, will show whether Peyton and the client actually leave feedback there before the whole team depends on it.
try: When ECA's next preview goes out, turn on comments, invite Peyton and Vince to comment directly on the page, and ask Peyton afterward what was easier or harder than Figma. Decide on the seats after that.
